en: The Commentary on the *Mayūraśataka* composed by Harivaṃśaśarman, together with the commentary of Harivaṃśaśarman.
The Hundred Verses on the Sun.
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Sun.

Having bowed with devotion to the hundred-petaled lotus of the feet of the glorious Gāyatrī, I compose this commentary on the *Raviśataka*, which is supremely pure, for the sake of its mother, the collection of the Vedas.
May he graciously awaken my intellect; and may that Śrī, who is the beauty of the arrangement of the lineage, [be present].
According to the *Medinī* lexicon, *bhāratī* refers to the goddess of speech, to a straight tree, to Lakṣmī, and also to the means for the attainment of the three goals of human life (*trivarga*).

Surrounded by those who are preeminent in their abundance of wakefulness, this awakening is the sole cause for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra; it destroys darkness just as the fierce sun destroys the lotus.
Where is the flavorful *Rasavatī*, and where is my very feeble intellect, O Peacock Sarasvatī?
Nevertheless, with my limited understanding, this is composed by me for the benefit of my son, according to my own best judgment.
From Gopāladeva, that twice-born man Harivaṃśaśarman was born on earth in the city of Yavacchala;
may this commentary, composed by him for the delight of the young, spread joy among the virtuous. (4)
Mayūraśarman, the poet, offered his benediction and then described the rays of the sun at dawn.

Regarding the passage beginning with *jambha*: the connection [of the words] is as follows: "May the *bhānavīyāḥ*—the *bhanavaḥ*, which are rays (*kiraṇāḥ*) related to the sun (*sūrya*)—be for your (*vaḥ*) prosperity (*vibhūtyai*), that is, for your sovereignty (*aiśvaryāya*).
According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*, "the two *bhanū*s are the rays and the light.
Alternatively, the vowel *a* [in *bhanavaḥ*] may be separated [to form *bhanu-vaḥ*].

"Aḥ" refers to Viṣṇu; his "vibhūti" (manifestation) is the sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the other powers. Because there is no difference between Viṣṇu and Sūrya, the meaning is that this is for the sake of attaining liberation through the attainment of identity with Viṣṇu. To the question, "What is this sovereignty of *aṇimā* and so forth?", he says:

"Atomicity (*aṇimā*), levity (*laghimā*), reach (*prāpti*), efficacy (*prākāmya*), magnanimity (*mahimā*), as well as lordship (*īśitā*), mastery (*vaśitā*), and the power to resolve desires (*kāmāvasāyitā*)."
"Bhūti-vibhūti" refers to the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*, according to Amara;
or alternatively, "aḥ" refers to Viṣṇu.

His adversary is Garuḍa; his *vibhūti* is the sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā*. For that [vibhūti], he is called *A*; likewise, Viṣṇu is designated by this single syllable as both a negation (*niṣedha*) and the imperishable (*avyaya*). Furthermore, *vi* refers to a bird (*vihaga*), and *vī* refers to Lakṣmī. Alternatively, *aviḥ* means the sun; his *vibhūti* is his sovereignty, meaning for the sake of attaining liberation through identification with the sun (*sūryasārūpya-mukti*). Or again, *aviḥ* means a mountain; his *vibhūti* is its abundance, because a mountain is the source of various substances.
According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*: "The word *avi* denotes a mountain, a ram, the sun, a male mouse, and a lotus."

*Bhūti* may mean the attainment of ashes (*bhasmasaṃpatti*), or according to the *Dharani*, "the ornament of Kali. Alternatively, that which becomes a distinction is *bhūti*; *na vibhūtiḥ* is *avibhūtiḥ*. For that *avibhūtyai*—meaning for non-rebirth, that is, for liberation. Of what nature are they? The rays (*bhānavaḥ*) seem to bear the thick vermilion dust arising from the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of Indra’s elephant, Airāvata—that is, the enemy of Jambha, the specific Daitya; "arising from" means produced by the impulse of the wind from that [globe].

"Sindūrareṇu" means the powder of vermilion (sindūra). "Sāndra-sindūrareṇu" refers to that thick and dense powder of vermilion. Bearing that thick powder of vermilion as if they were holding it, for this very reason they are red, that is, of a crimson hue. Indeed, the substance of vermilion is applied to the frontal globes (kumbha) of elephants—the location of the ichor—for the sake of beauty.
The sun also rises in the eastern direction, and Airāvata likewise resides right there.

The word *iva* is used here in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), for such descriptions are dear to poets. Furthermore, how are these rays characterized? They are red in color, as if adhered to by masses—that is, streams—of the liquid flow of mineral ores from the slopes of the Sunrise Mountain (*udayagiri*). Alternatively, "masses" refers to the streams, ridges, or continuous lines of the red chalk (*gairika*) ore on the mountain's slope—the ridge of that eastern peak—and they are red through the collections of its liquid essence.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *ogha* refers to a multitude, the current of water, and the instruction for rapid dancing;
here too, its red color is to be inferred. Furthermore, this word *dhātu* specifically denotes "mineral" (*aṅgasthi*) and "red ochre" (*gairika*), according to the *Viśvakośa*.

This word *dhātu* is used here specifically for "bone" (*asthi*) and "red ochre" (*gairika*), as well as for "the front of an army," "a shoulder," "a continuous stream," and "the five states of existence" (*gatipañcaka*), according to the *Nānārthakoṣa*.
Furthermore, the *Prakāśa* lexicon states: "The masculine [form] *dhātu* refers to a rush, two tastes, a cloth, a mountain, and a liquid."

Furthermore, what are they like? They are red (aruṇa), that is, crimson, like the luster (ruk) of a forest of lotuses (kamalavana)—that is, the beauty (śobhā) of a forest of red lotuses—as they arrive and rise at the same time, at one and the same moment. Here, by the word "lotus" (kamala), the red lotus is indicated by way of synecdoche. Furthermore, what are they like? Illuminating—that is, lighting up—the world (bhuvana). Furthermore, what are they like? Fresh (abhinava), new, belonging to the morning; or else, the prefix *abhi-* should be analyzed separately [as meaning "toward"]. What [world] is it?

"Bhuvanam" refers to that world (*bhuvana*) which possesses stars (*nakṣatra*) for its attainment (*abhisaṃnakṣatra*). Here, the prefix *abhi* is used in the sense of "attaining" (*abhyarthe*), not in the sense of "toward" (*abhi*). It is "starless" (*na-bhi*) because of the rising of the sun;
for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *bha* may mean a ray or Venus; *bham* is proclaimed to be a star.

Alternatively, it is that world in which there is no fear (*bhī*) or terror (*bhaya*); here, due to the absence of darkness, there is no cause for fear anywhere, since fear ceases upon the rising of the sun. Or else, it is that action in which there is no fear or terror; here, the neuter gender is used as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇe*).
"Bhītiḥ, bhīḥ, sādhvasam, and bhayam" are synonyms according to Amara.
"That which consists of three *mra*, *bha*, *na*, *ya*, and *na* gaṇas, with pauses at the third and seventh syllables, is called *Sragdharā*," so it is stated in the *Chandomañjarī*. //1//

Because the rays of the sun illuminate the lotus grove, he says "bhakti" and so forth: may those rays—*karāḥ*, meaning *kiraṇāḥ* (beams)—of *bhāskara*, the sun, bring about (*kriyāsuḥ*) for you (*vaḥ*, i.e., *yuṣmākam* or *yuṣmabhyam*) auspiciousness (*kalyāṇam*), that is, welfare (*maṅgalam*).
Alternatively, may they bring about auspiciousness that is imperishable (*akṣayam*), meaning indestructible (*avināśam*).
"Kalyāṇa" means inexhaustible (*akṣaya*) and golden (*svarṇa*), and it also means auspicious (*maṅgala*), according to the *Viśva* lexicon. (52cd, p.
51) What are these rays?
"The opening of the lotus forest" (*kamalavanodghāṭana*): a forest of lotuses (*kamala*)—that is, of *padma* flowers—is a "lotus forest" (*kamalavana*); the "opening" (*udghāṭana*) of that.

The connection is: "They make manifest" means "they perform. Of what kind are the rays? They are as if desirous of attracting—that is, desirous of seizing—the Fortune (Lakṣmī) in order to give it to one who is bowed down with devotion (*bhaktiprahva*). It is well known that Fortune dwells in the lotus; for this very reason, her name is called *Padmālayā*.
The etymological meaning is: she whose dwelling (*ālaya*) or home is the lotus (*padma*), thus she is named *Padmālayā*.

Of what kind is Fortune? She is hidden within the interior of the hollow of the bud-cottage (*mukulapuṭakuṭīkoṭarakroḍalīnā*); [that is,] within the interior of the bud, which is the pericarp of the lotus.

A *puṭa* is a bud-cup; the *kuṭī* (hut) of that bud-cup is its innermost chamber, for the bud-cup itself is like a hut. Its *koṭara* is the interior space, and its *kroḍa* is the central part. [The bird] is hidden, meaning situated there. According to Śāśvata: "In the case of *śobhā*, *sampatti*, and *padmā*, *lakṣmī* means *śrī* (fortune/glorious beauty). (162ab, p. 13)

Other rays (karāḥ) as well draw forth Lakṣmī who resides within the house; there is a pun on the word *kara*, for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *kara* [is used] for hailstones, a ray, a hand, tax, and an elephant's trunk."

Alternatively, the bud-cup itself is the small jar (*kuṭikumbha*); gems and other valuables are hidden within the hollow interior of its belly, for it is said that such things are placed inside a jar. For this very reason, it is called a "treasure-jar" (*nidhānakumbha*).
According to the *Prakāśa*, the word *kumbha* is used in the masculine sense for a small jar (*kuṭī*), for Citragupta, for a jar, and for a house.

Of what nature were they? Their rays were like the darkness of the form of Time (*kālākārāndhakāra*). They were capable of destroying the terror of the world fallen into [that] darkness. "Kālākāra" means a dark form; that is the darkness, which is gloom. Alternatively, *kāla* is Yama; his "form" (*ākāra*) is his body, thus "the form of Time" (*kālākāra*). Darkness like that is "the darkness of the form of Time" (*kālākārāndhakāra*), because of the similarity [of the rays] to Yama due to his black color. Or else, *kāla* is Mahākāla, whose body is of great form; darkness like that is "the darkness of the form of Time" (*kālākārāndhakāra*), as it is also [like] Mahākāla.

Because of its black color, there is a similarity [to death]; alternatively, *kāla* means death (*mṛtyu*), and that which has the form of, or is equal to, that [death] and is also darkness is "the darkness of the form of time" (*kālākārāndhakāra*). Because darkness brings about fear for all beings, it shares a similarity with death. Regarding the words *mahākāla*, *yama*, and *mṛtyu*, as well as *kāla* in the sense of "time" and "black," the lexicographer Śāśvata states: "The word *kāla* [denotes] time and black. (367cd, p. 29)

The face (*ānana*) of that darkness shaped like Time (*kālākārāndhakāra*)—the world has fallen into it—and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the fear (*sādhvasa*) of that [world] is its dispersal (*ṭana*). That which is skillful (*kalya*) therein—or rather, that dawn (*kalya*) from which comes the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), meaning the end, of the fear of the world fallen into the face of that darkness shaped like Time; such is that dawn. For through the rising of rays, the time of daybreak occurs.

Alternatively, those who have destroyed the world’s fear of the darkness of time and form are "kalya," meaning healthy and free from disease; for through the rising of his rays, the destruction of darkness occurs, and those who depend upon his rays become healthy as well. *Kalyam* means dawn or preparedness; according to Śāśvata, *kalya* refers to being free from disease or being capable. (24ab, p. 3)

Of what kind [are they]? They are those whose *ruci*—meaning beauty or splendor—is like that of a *kiśalaya*, a fresh leaf; thus, "possessing such [beauty]. Because of their reddish color, there is a similarity with a fresh leaf. Hands, too, are comparable to fresh leaves. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "*Ruci*" is used for a ray, beauty, attachment, and desire. (2) (7ab, p. 30) He describes the rays by means of their heat, saying:
"In the wombs," etc.

May the rays—the feet—of Bradhna, the Sun, protect you most intensely; that is, may they guard you. According to Dhanañjaya, *bradhna* refers to Pūṣan, Aryaman, and Ravi. Of what nature are these? They are the "feet of Bradhna," bearing—that is, maintaining—a heat as if born from the fatigue of a continuous journey. From the fatigue of a continuous journey, there arises an excessive exhaustion from traveling on the road; the feet of the Sun, however, naturally maintain heat, and not [merely] from the fatigue of a journey. Therefore, the poet employs this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), imagining it as if produced from the fatigue of a journey.

There is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *pāda*, as it signifies both "feet" (*caraṇa*)—which bear the appearance of having been seen due to the fatigue of the journey—and "mountain foot" (*pratyantaparvata*). According to Medinīkara: "The word *pāda* denotes a quarter, a mountain foot, a bordering mountain, a foot, and a ray.
Furthermore, how are they qualified?

The three worlds (*tribhuvana*) are his own realm; his abode (*bhavana*) is his house. The courtyard (*prāṅgaṇa*) of that abode of the three worlds is the region of space (*ākāśadeśa*). In that courtyard of the abode of the three worlds, [the rays] have proceeded (*pravṛtta*) without succession (*niṣparyāya*), that is, without sequence (*kramarahita*). While the feet (*pāda*, i.e., rays) of others proceed in succession, the feet of the Sun (*bradhna*) have proceeded by way of yoga without succession, that is, without sequence. Thus, the feet—meaning the rays—of others also move within the courtyard of the house. According to Amara: "Succession (*paryāya*) means turn (*avasara*) or order (*krama*)" (147b, p. 422).

Furthermore, what are they like? They have fallen—attained—at the same time, simultaneously, both within the centers (garbha) of the lotuses (ambhoruha), that is, the lotuses (padma), and also upon the mountain peaks (śikhari). Upon what kind of peaks? Upon those with sharp points (śitāgra); "śita" means sharp, and "agra" refers to their summits. Furthermore, what are they like?

At the beginning of the day—that is, at its rising in the morning—and likewise at the time of the day's conclusion, at the time of its ending in the evening, [the sun] is of one form, of equal appearance; it is red-colored both in the evening and in the morning. Thus, according to another text: "The sun is copper-colored at rising, and it is indeed copper-colored at setting as well. The word "of the day" (*vāsarasya*) connects with both [phrases] by way of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpa*) maxim. //3//
He describes the rays by way of their similarity to threads, saying "prabhāsyati" (it shall shine).

Those rays—*marīcayaḥ*—may they grant (*diśantu*) or bestow (*dadantu*) *maṅgala*, that is, prosperity (*śreyaḥ*), to you (*vaḥ*) constantly (*śaśvat*), meaning repeatedly or always. According to the *Prakāśa*, the word *śaśvat* refers to both "always" and "again. Alternatively, may they grant *maṅgala*, which is the accomplishment of all aims (*sarvārthasādhana*).
*Maṅgala* is used for prosperity, as well as for the white *durvā* grass, which is also called *maṅgalā*. (79cd, p. 154)
And it is stated in the *Viśva* lexicon that "it is also proclaimed as an auspicious omen for the accomplishment of all goals" (80ab, p. 154).
Who are "those"? They are the rays of the sun, which has scorching light (*tigmarociḥ*).

The connection is with the word "those": [the rays] which he spreads out—that is, extends—like threads (*taṃtūn*), meaning like strands (*sūtrāṇi*), in such a way that they are not thin (*atanūn*), so that they may be non-different (*ananyaṃ*) [from him].
"Pāda, Ruci, Marīci, and Bha are synonyms for *dhanañjaya*.

(49c, p-23) Here, the word *yathā* has the sense of *iva* ("like"). What is the purpose [of this]? At the time of dawn, when darkness—that is, obscurity—has vanished or perished, one should behold or look upon the worlds as threads or as woven garments (*vāravṛti*) from which the feet have departed. In what kind of darkness? In that which possesses a luster or beauty like an upper garment (*uttarīya*); that is, in that which has a splendor resembling an upper garment.
The commentary states: "Up until before dawn" means "in the interval.

What are those rays like? Immediately at that moment, having become dense—that is, having spread out—they "bring about the sky," meaning they manifest it. Alternatively, having become dense, they "bring about the garment" (ambara); thus there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *ambara*.
For the various meanings [of *ambara*] include "fragrant substance," "the sky," and "clothing. (*Ambaraṃ vyomavastrayoḥ*, according to the *Nānārtha*).
What kind of garment? Vast with rows of quarters that become increasingly clear. The quarters—the ten directions—become increasingly (*krama*) clear, stainless, and white;

[the compound] *kramaviśadadaśāśāḥ* refers to those [directions]. It is vast because it possesses rows (*āvali*) of them. Furthermore, the garment itself becomes vast through its ten [stripes]. The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *āśā* is used for both thirst and direction. (14c, p-168)
According to the *Medinī* lexicon, the word *ambara* denotes ten things, including the wick of a lamp, the end of a garment, the earth, and a woman.
Furthermore, how is it qualified? It is *alam*, meaning "exceedingly" or "extremely," and *alam* also means "pure. Thus, it is *ambara* (the sky/cloth) that is *emendambala*.

Alternatively, it is an adjective; that in which there is no stain (*mala*)—that is, sin (*pāpa*)—is "stainless" (*amala*), meaning sinless. Or, it is an adjective qualifying "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*), for auspiciousness arises from being sinless. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *mala* denotes sin, excrement, a Śūdra, and a miser."
Alternatively, *atanu* means "not small," that is to say, "vast" because of its all-pervasiveness, or it refers to a specific kind of garment (*ambara-viśeṣa*).
According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *tanu* [is used] for the body, for 'slender,' for 'small,' and also for 'rare,' as a term to be expressed. (18ab, p.

86). The sense is that the sun, having seen the worlds without clothing, provides them with garments and thus performs a service for others. Since cold is warded off even by a garment, the rays of the sun are also described as being of the nature of clothing because they ward off the cold; this is the pun (*dhvani*). //4//

"Subduing," and so forth. May the rising of the rays—the emergence of the beams—of the intensely radiant Sun (tīvrabhānu) be for the removal of what is not desired (anabhimatanude), that is, for the destruction of your enemies. "Abhimata" means desired; "not abhimata" is "anabhimata," meaning undesired or inauspicious; it refers to that which he removes.

"Premayati" means "he bestows love. [The word] *anabhimatanut* means "removing what is undesired"; here, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *nud* (in the sense of "to impel"). *Tīvrabhānuḥ* refers to one whose rays (*bhānavaḥ*) or splendors (*dīptayaḥ*) are intense (*tīvra*); or alternatively, *tīvra* is the sun (*bhānuḥ*), thus *tīvrabhānuḥ*. Regarding that *tīvrabhānoḥ*, the word *bhānu* means "splendor" or "the sun-maker" (*dinakara*); thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. What is he like? He is *gabhastyudgamaḥ* (arising from the hands/rays) and *ātāmraḥ* (reddish-brown). *Ātāmraḥ* means reddish on all sides (*ā-samantāt*) or slightly (*ā-īṣat*) copper-colored (*tāmraḥ*), i.e., red in hue. Regarding *ātāmraḥ*, the *Nānārtha* lexicon states: "*Āmraṃ* [is used] in the senses of 'redness' and 'copper.'"

Of what kind [is he]? He is as if his upward movement has already been performed by the fire (*pāvaka*) arisen from the *sūryakānti* stone—the "sun-stone" (*bhāsvadgrāva*), meaning the rock of the sun’s brilliance—due to the emergence of the rays (*gabhastyudgama*) of the radiant sun (*bhāsvat*). When a learned person (*śiṣṭa*) arrives, rising from one's seat is the conduct of the learned; thus, the meaning is that fire arises in the sun-stone upon contact with the rays of the rising sun. What was he doing? [He was] causing the medicinal herbs (*auṣadhī*)... [to flourish].

Supplanting and eclipsing the splendor of the sun, the herbs wither; for what kind of herbs? When the Lord of Herbs, the Moon—the Lord of Night—has his luster stolen away by the Sun and is thus distressed, they become as if devoid of light, their radiance departed out of grief. Furthermore, what does the Lord of the Dawn do? He reveals the stones of the Mountain of Sunrise, which appear as if they were dripping with the blood from the wounds of having their wings clipped. What are these stones like? They are as if streaming with the blood from the scars of their wings being severed.

The cutting off of a wing is *pakṣaccheda*; the wound from that is *pakṣacchedavraṇa*; the blood flowing from that is *pakṣacchedavraṇāsṛksrut*, [formed with] the *kvip* suffix. Like those [wounds], the word *dṛśat* (stone) is feminine; when the rising of the rays strikes the stone of the mountain of sunrise (*udayaparvata*), because of their reddish color, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that they are like streams of blood flowing forth. According to the Purāṇas, Indra indeed caused the cutting off of the wings of the mountains with his thunderbolt.

Alternatively, *gabhastyudgama* refers to the rising or emergence of the sun; that is, the sunrise. Of what kind [of sun]? Of the morning sun (*prātarindra*), the intensely radiant one (*tīvrabhānu*). That morning sun in which the rays (*bhānavaḥ*)—meaning intense or harsh beams—are present; of that [sun]. The rest is the same. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *gabhasti* occurs in the senses of 'ray,' 'the sun,' and 'Svāhā. According to the *Amarakośa*: "The words *bhanu*, *kara*, and *marīci* are feminine [and mean 'ray']. //5//

"Śrīrṇṇa," and so forth. May the rays (ghṛṇayaḥ) of that Gharmaṃśu, the Sun, quickly—that is, with speed—bring about (vidadhatu) a destruction (vighātam) of you (vaḥ), your multitudes (oghaiḥ). The root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*), and the root *bhāṣ* is used preceded by *abhi-*. Furthermore, since it is stated that the root *pūrvā* is remembered as being used in the sense of "placing" when preceded by *sam-*, the root *dhā* preceded by *vi-* here signifies "doing" (*karaṇam*). [The word] *agha-*...

He [is the one] who effects the warding off and destruction of evil—*agha* meaning sin or misdeed (*duṣkṛta*), according to Amara; *gharma* means heat; he whose rays (*aṃśu*) or beams are heat is *Gharmāṃśu*. Of what kind is that *Gharmāṃśu*? His activity is unimpeded because it is struck by intense, thick, and dense compassion (*ghṛṇā*). That [compassion] is both "thick" (*ghana*) and "dense" (*sāndra*).

*Ghṛṇā* means compassion (*kṛpā*). Thus, *ghanaghṛṇā* refers to intense compassion; alternatively, it is compassion like that of a dense cloud (*ghana*), for it nourishes all the world. Or, it is *ghanaghṛṇā* because it is both dense (*ghana*) and compassionate (*ghṛṇā*), being vast in extent.

Or, it is *ghanaghṛṇā* because it is both dense (*ghana*)—meaning immovable—and compassionate (*ghṛṇā*, i.e., *kṛpā*). Internally, within the mind, there is accomplishment (*siddhi*); externally, it is *ghanaghṛṇā* because it transcends all the world.
The destruction of that [merit], caused by another's influence such as greed and so forth, occurs through an internal doubling of intense compassion;
this is the destruction of that [merit] through an internal doubling of intense compassion.

He whose nature is free from the obstruction of killing—that is, his activity is devoid of violence—is "struck by an internal, doubly intense compassion" (*antardviguṇaghanaghṛṇānighna*). Here, *niḥ* means "without," so *nirvighnavṛttiḥ* means "one whose activity is unobstructed. The meaning is that the compassion of that Sun-god is free from obstacles such as greed or the like, being under the sway of mercy alone. According to Amara, *kāruṇya*, *karuṇā*, and *ghṛṇā* are synonyms for compassion.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, "ghana" means dense, thick, far-reaching, long, broad, or even a type of mustaka grass.
Of that [Lord], who is the sun (gharmāśu) [to the world], there is one whose feet, hands, and nose have withered away due to being afflicted by diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

Furthermore, the connection is that he joins them together again or makes them new once more. "Ghrāṇāṅghripāṇayaḥ" means the nose (ghrāṇa), feet (aṅghri), and hands (pāṇi). "Śīrṇaghrāṇāṅghripāṇayaḥ" refers to those whose noses, feet, and hands are shattered or fallen away; here, *ghrāṇa* means the nose and *aṅghri* means the foot.
According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The root *ghrā* is used in the sense of smelling and for the nose.

The meaning is that the Sun, by removing [the disease], makes those suffering from the wasting disease of leprosy free from illness. What is he doing? He is making them light, that is, making them healthy. Of what nature is this Sun, the possessor of heat-rays (*gharmāṃśu*)? He is the One (*eka*).

"Advitīyaḥ" means that there is no other like him; or, "ekaḥ" means he is the foremost; or, "ekaḥ" means he alone, as the *Prakāśa* lexicon states: "The word 'eka' is used in three senses: alone, foremost, and another. Of what kind [are they]? They have indistinct, gurgling sounds (*gharghara*) produced by their "apaghanas"—that is, their vocal organs such as the throat, lips, and palate—which are characterized by wounds (*vraṇin*).

"Gharghara" refers to the sound of a camel's neck or the sound of a flowing stream; those whose indistinct and unclear sounds are like that are "ghargharāvyaktaghoṣāḥ. This means they are uttering cries of distress like those of people suffering from diseases such as leprosy. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "Gharghara, however, is used for the sound of a camel or a loud noise."

Furthermore, of what nature were they? They were "long-obsessed by floods of evil" (*aghaughair dīrghāghrātān*), meaning they were excessively filled with multitudes of sins (*pāpasamūhaiḥ*)—that is, from various great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), diseases such as leprosy and others emerged from them. Alternatively, they were "long-obsessed by floods of suffering" (*aghaughair duḥkhasamūhair dīrghāghrātān*); for the *Viśvakośa* states: "Agha means sin, calamity, and old age. Of what nature were they? They were "those to whom the water-offering was given by the hosts of Siddhas"—that is, by the assemblies (*saṃghāḥ*) or multitudes of Siddhas, gods, and sages; those Siddhas to whom the water-offering (*argha*) was given are called "those to whom the water-offering was given" (*dattārghāḥ*). For the *Viśvakośa* states: "Argha means worship and the root of the *vighu* plant. //6//

With the left [verse] as an illustration, he describes the rays with the words beginning "bibhrāṇāḥ" and so forth: "May the sun-like rays (haridasvāḥ), the beams belonging to the Sun, remove— that is, distance— your hardships (kṛcchrāṇi) and miseries."
*Dīdhiti*, *bhānu*, *ruma*, and *aṃśu* are synonyms for the sun, according to Dhanañjaya.

*Kaṣṭa*, *kṛcchra*, and *ābhīla* are synonyms for difficulty or distress, according to Amara. *Haridaśva* refers to the Sun (Sūrya), whose horses (*turaga*) are green (*harita*) in color; or alternatively, he is called *haridaśva* because his horses are like the *harit* grass in color, owing to their green hue.

Equanimity; or else, *haridaśva* refers to one whose horses (*vājin*)—a specific type of steed—are green (*harita*). The word *hari* has multiple meanings: it denotes a direction (the quarter), a color, grass, or a specific type of horse.
These [horses] belonging to Haridaśva are called *haridaśvāḥ*.
According to Amara, "the rays of the sun are called *bhāsvat-sapta-aśva* and *harid-aśva*.

Of what nature are these rays? They are "those who have mocked Hari with the ease of their rising" (*ucchrāya-helā-vahasita-harayaḥ*). This means that Hari (Viṣṇu) was mocked or ridiculed by them through the ease (*helā*)—that is, the lack of effort—of their upward movement (*ucchrāya*). Alternatively, it refers to those whose easeful play (*helā-vilāsa*) in rising mocks Hari; thus, the meaning is that their height is equal to that of Viṣṇu.

The word *helāva* means "playful" (*vilāsya*) according to the various meanings [of the lexicon]. What are they qualified as? The rays (*aṃśavaḥ*), bearing (*vibhraṇāḥ*) a dwarfishness (*vāmanatva*) or hunchbackedness (*kharbatva*) at first—that is, previously—become hunchbacked at their initial rising. There is a pun (*śleṣa*) with the word "Vāmana": for Hari also, in order to destroy Bali, was bearing the state of being Vāmana, that is, the incarnation as Vāmana.
"Vāmana is proclaimed as the third [incarnation] when Viṣṇu has become dwarfed," according to Śaśvata.

Furthermore, what are they [the incarnations] like? Immediately thereafter—that is, following Vāmana—they were likewise *prāṃśavaḥ*, meaning tall. Again, what are they like? Following that—that is, after having become tall—they were *krāntākāśāntarālāḥ*, meaning those by whom the intermediate space of the sky (*ākāśāntarāla*) was traversed or leaped over. Regarding this, Amara states: "The word *atyantara* is a synonym for *antarāla* (intermediate space)."

Furthermore, what are they like? Immediately after that—that is, immediately following the traversing of the intermediate space of the sky—they fill the ten directions; that is, they pervade the ten numbered quarters. Just as Hari, after assuming the form of Vāmana, took on the form of Trivikrama and became tall, and thereafter traversed the intermediate space and subsequently filled the ten directions—thus [the author] distinguishes them by their equality with Hari. Furthermore, what are they like? Swiftly and quickly pervading (āśuvānāḥ) the entire universe (viśvaṃ jagat);
[the root] *aś* means "to pervade. Having done what?

"Having snatched away from Dhvāntada," meaning having seized [it] from him; "as if from whom? "As if from Vali, the enemy of the gods (devadviṣ)," that is, from the Asura Vali; "on the fifth day. The Purāṇa states: Viṣṇu first assumed the form of Vāmana, and immediately thereafter, having taken the form of Trivikrama and snatched the universe away from the Daitya Vali, he pervaded the entire world. //7//

"By the intense," and so forth: may those rays—or "mayūkhas" (which, according to Śāśvata, denote both light and rays)—of the sun, the steed of the sky, grant or bestow *śarma* (well-being) upon you (*vaḥ*).
Śāśvata states: "The word *mayūkha* is said to mean light, as well as time and a ray."
He whose rays (aṃśavaḥ) or beams (kiraṇāḥ) are harsh (kharāḥ) and intense (tīkṣṇāḥ) is Kharāṃśu; or alternatively, he who is both harsh and intense, and is the sun (sūrya), is Kharāṃśu.
Regarding him, the Haimakoṣa states: "The sun, Āditya, Savitṛ, Aryaman, Kharasahasra, Aṃśu, and Raśmi are synonyms."
The *Viśvakośa* states: "Aṃśu" means rays;
"śarma" means hundreds of happinesses, according to Amara.

Alternatively, "su-kha" refers to a beautiful heaven (*svarga*). Or, "su" is used in the sense of excellence, and "kha" means heaven; thus, "sukha" means a beautiful heaven. Alternatively, "su" is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) used in the senses of excellence, honor, intensity, abundance, or difficulty; these are prepositions (*upasarga*) that function in these various meanings.

The moon is in the sky; the sense-faculties are in the void; "ka" refers to the ether, heaven, and happiness—so says Prakāśa. What are those rays? They are characterized by an intense, exceeding, and inherent ruddiness.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: they "perform" (*vidadhati*)—that is, they "bring about" (*kurvanti*)—the "intensity" (*vahala*), meaning the abundance (*bahutva*), of the redness, that is, the state of being red-colored, of Aruṇa, the charioteer of the Sun, by virtue of his being red-colored.
Aruṇa is red-colored; the rays of the Sun are also red-colored. Therefore, the meaning is that the redness of Aruṇa becomes exceedingly intense due to its contact with the rays of the Sun.
According to Amara, *ativela*, *bhṛśa*, *atyartha*, and *atimātra* are synonyms for "excessive" (*udgāra*).

Furthermore, what are those rays which, when the head is shaken, possess the luster of blood from wounds caused by the bit? The connection is "those rays are indeed to be taken. The horses of the chariot are *rathāśvāḥ*; their faces are *rathāśvānanāni*; upon them (*teṣu*), of the head (*mūrghnaḥ*)—that is, of the crown (*śirasaḥ*).

*Uddhūti* means shaking; *mūrddoddhūtiḥ* refers to the shaking of the head. When that shaking of the head occurs, a wound or sore (*kṣata*) is produced by the bit (*khalīna*), which is known as *kaliāra*; this is a "bit-wound. From that [wound] comes blood (*rudhira*), and those rays whose luster (*ruca*) is like that blood are "possessing the luster of blood from a bit-wound" (*khalīnakṣatarudhirarucaḥ*). Since a wound occurs in the mouth when horses shake their heads, there is a comparison with blood here because the morning sunbeams possess a red color. The word *khalīna* refers to the bit that is fixed (*līna*) in the opening of the mouth (*kha*). According to Amara, *karikā* is another term for the bit, used in both genders.

Furthermore, the connection is as follows: "Which are those rays that extend—that is, perform—the state of being crest-ornaments (*śekhara*), the flower-garlands adorning the heads, of the *śailas*, the mountains? What kind of rays? They are 'those which have resorted to the peaks' (*śritaśikharāḥ*); that is, those rays of the morning sun which have taken refuge in the *śikharas*, the summits or upper parts of the *śikharins*, the mountains; for at dawn, the sun's rays take shelter merely upon the peaks of the mountains.
For this very reason, there is a comparison here between the rays and a flower-garland used as a head-ornament. [As Amara states: 'A peak is called both *śikhā* and *śikhara*.'"

Of what nature are the rays? They are *preṅkhantaḥ*, meaning they illuminate within the *khe*, the sky. Again, of what nature are they? They are *khacitadinamukhāḥ*, meaning those by which the face of the day—the morning—is *khacitam*, or rendered variegated. //8//
He describes the rays as "Gotvena" (by way of being rays):

"Dattānandā" and so forth. May the rays (*gāvaḥ*)—the beams—of the radiant one (*dīptāṃśoḥ*), that is, of the Sun (*sūryasya*), produce for you (*vaḥ*)—to you—an immeasurable (*aparimitām*) and exceeding (*bahutarām*) joy (*prītim*) and gladness (*harṣam*), in such a way that it is the most excellent among the purifying (*pāvanānām*). The meaning is: may they grant sons, wives, wealth, and other objects of pleasure and enjoyment.
The *Amara-kośa* states: "The joy arising from my affection is *harṣa*.

Alternatively, it may mean: "May they produce immeasurable—that is, uninterrupted—affection or happiness," for liberation (*mukti*) is defined as the state of being a continuous stream of bliss. Or again, it may mean: "Among the purifiers, [may they be] the most excellent," and furthermore, "may they produce immeasurable affection."

The two actions: [the phrase] *dīptāṃśoḥ* means one whose rays (*aṃśavaḥ*) or beams (*kiraṇāḥ*) are blazing (*dīptāḥ*) or beautiful (*śobhitāḥ*). Alternatively, *dīptaṃśuḥ* refers to the Sun (*sūrya*), for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *aṃśuḥ* denotes the sun, a ray, and light. Or else, it refers to one whose rays or splendor (*prabhā*) are blazing; [the genitive] *tasya aṃśoḥ* [refers to him].
According to the *Medinīkośa*, the word *pratta* refers to rays.

Furthermore, other cows—the milch-cows—being pure (*pravitratvāt*), produce even greater joy as if they were the very purifier (*pavitra*) among purifiers. This is a *śleṣa* (pun) expressed by the word "cow" (*go*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *go* is masculine when meaning a bull, a ray, or a thunderbolt; it is feminine when meaning a cow, the eye, an arrow, a direction, the earth, or used in the plural."

Of what nature are the rays? They are those which are drawn in and emitted at the appropriate time—that is, during the seasons of summer and the rains. According to the tradition, it rains in the monsoon season by taking up water [during the summer] through those rays drawn in and emitted at the appropriate time.
Manu says: "From the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; from that, living beings.
And Raghu says: "The sun takes up the water with its rays and emits it a thousandfold."

In the case of the cow (*dhenu*), at the appropriate time—both morning and evening—those [milkings] which have been drawn and those which have been released, and by means of those milks (*payaḥ*) that were drawn and released at the proper times, she grants joy to the offspring (*prajā*), meaning the calves; and to the animals such as cows and buffaloes, she releases the milk from her belly at the time of their desire and does not release it at the time of their non-desire; this is the nature of being an animal (*paśutva*). "Milk" (*payaḥ*) means both "milk" (*kṣīra*) and "water" (*nīra*); thus says the *Prakāśa*. And according to the *Medinī*: "The word *prajā* refers to offspring and the world."

Furthermore, of what nature are these rays? In the forenoon, at the time of morning, they are scattered—that is, spread out—in every direction, in all ten directions. Cows also, having been released from their bonds in the forenoon, become spread out in every direction. Furthermore, of what nature are they?

The rays, at the end of the day—that is, at evening—become subject to withdrawal; they undergo dissolution. According to the traditional teaching (*āgama*), the rays of the sun, having issued from the solar orb at the time of dawn, re-enter it at the conclusion of the day. Cows likewise become gathered together in a single pen at the end of the day. Furthermore, what are they like?

"Rays" (*raśmayaḥ*) refers to those that extend for a long time, over a vast duration; "long suffering" (*dīrghaduḥkha*) is that which is difficult to endure for a long time. That from which this arises—that is, its source or place of origin—is the "source of long suffering. "Existence" (*bhava*) is synonymous with *saṃsāra*. Fear (*bhaya*) is trembling; thus, "fear of existence, the source of long suffering" (*dīrghaduḥkhaprabhavabhavabhaya*). That very thing is the "ocean" (*udadhi*). Crossing over it is "crossing" (*uttāra*), meaning going forth. Like boats (*nāvaḥ*)—that is, like ships—in that [ocean], they are "boats for crossing over the fear of existence, the source of long suffering" (*dīrghaduḥkhaprabhavabhavabhayodadhyuttāranāvaḥ*).

In the worship of the sun’s rays, liberation from saṃsāra does not occur; whereas through the worship of the cow, liberation from saṃsāra occurs—this is the similarity. Alternatively, the similarity lies in the fact that by holding onto the tail of a cow, one crosses the ocean. //9//

"Vandhatyādi" and so forth. The construction is as follows: may those rays of the sun (dinakara-kiraṇāḥ), the solar beams, become—so that it may be certain (nirvilpaṃ) and without doubt—the banners (ketavaḥ), that is, the causes of destruction, for your "kalmaṣa," meaning either sin (pāpa) or a particular hell (naraka-viśeṣa). Regarding the word *kalmaṣa*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "Kalmaṣa, kilviṣa, and kliva denote sin; in the masculine, it refers to a specific hell."

Who are those [rays] which are the rays of the sun that bring about the awakening—the supreme awakening, that is to say, the knowledge of Brahman—of the worlds? The sense is that by resorting to the rays of the sun, one attains liberation. Of what nature is this awakening? It is the sole cause, the unique cause, for the destruction—that is, the annihilation—of bondage, which is *māyā*.
According to Amara, the word *eka* means "sole," "principal," "other than," or "exclusive."

The meaning is that for those who possess the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), there is no further dwelling in a womb. Of what kind of people? Of those whose hands are joined in salutation upon their heads due to the "essence" (*rasa*)—that is, the passion (*rāga*)—of bowing (*nati*) to the worlds. For those whose hands are thus joined in *saṃdhyā* (the twilight devotion), the joining of hands (*añjali*) is like a lotus bud; the implied suggestion (*dhvani*) is that it is appropriate for them to attain awakening (*prabodha*).

How does it bring about awakening? To this he says: "Like a vast cluster of lotuses. A "cluster of lotuses" (*ambhojakhaṇḍa*) is a grove of lotuses (*padma*); a "vast" (*vipula*) and great (*mahat*) cluster of lotuses is a "vast cluster of lotuses" (*vipulāmbhojakhaṇḍa*). It is as if [the mind] were bound by that.

Of what nature are the rays of the sun? They are wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) for the vast and expansive aspirations of one’s own mind. "One’s own mind" (*svacitta*) refers to the mind itself; its breadth and extensiveness is "the expansiveness of one’s own mind" (*svacittapṛthimā*); and the aspirations that are even more extensive than that expansiveness are the "wish-fulfilling trees of those aspirations," because they fulfill whatever is prayed for. Alternatively, the rays of the sun, together with the beds of abundant lotuses, bring about the awakening of the world from its sleep.

"Vipulāmbhojakhaṇḍasya āśā" means the vast expanse of the lotus-cluster; here, the word "iva" (as if) has the sense of "eva" (indeed). Just as the rays of the sun bring about the awakening of the world and the lotus-clusters, so too does the "āśā" (desire)—for Amara states that "āśā" means both "direction" and "thirst"—bring about the breaking of the sleep of people. In this context, "bandha" refers to sleep. Therefore, of what kind of people? Of those who, immediately after the breaking of their sleep, have bound their hands in the *añjali* gesture of twilight upon their heads, as if it were a flight of stairs. //10//

"Dhārārāya" means: may the rays (raśmayaḥ) or beams (kiraṇāḥ) of the intensely shining sun (tīvrabhānoḥ sūryasya) protect (trāyantām)—that is, preserve—yourselves from sin (kalmaṣāt), meaning from evil (pāpāt) or from hell (kalmaṣānām narakāt). [The root] trai- is used in the sense of protecting; it takes the second person plural middle voice (ātmanepada). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "Kalmaṣam is neuter in the sense of a fault (kilviṣe), and masculine when referring to a particular hell."
*Tīvrabhānuḥ* means one whose heat (*uṣman*) and rays (*kiraṇa*) are intense; or, since *tīvra* is [intense] and *bhānu* is the sun (*sūrya*), it is *tīvrabhānuḥ*.
Regarding this, Medinī states: "The word *bhānu* refers to a ray or the sun."

Of what nature are the rays? They are "divasamukhasukhāḥ," meaning they bring pleasure at the beginning of the day, that is, in the morning. It is fitting that the rays of the sun, which possess a coolness at the time of dawn, should provide such comfort. Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are "dhanāyāpadirāyaḥ. *Dhanāyā* means the desire for wealth; *āpad* means calamity, so called because it is a cause for falling downward. *Irāyaḥ* refers to streams of gold or riches—Medinī states: "The word *rāḥ* is masculine and denotes both gold and wealth. Thus, they are those who dispel the calamity of the desire for wealth.
Alternatively, in times of distress when there is a lack of wealth, "for wealth" (*dhanāya*) means for the sake of obtaining riches; "streams of riches" (*rāyo dhārāḥ*) refers to streams of property.

Or, in times of distress such as drought, "for wealth" means for the sake of cattle-wealth, that is, for the purpose of procuring grass for the cows; here "streams of riches" (*rāyo dhārāḥ*) refers to the streams of clouds, because they are the cause of rain.
As it is said in the Purāṇa: "From the Sun, rain is born."
*Rudra* states that *dhana* refers to both cattle-wealth (*godhana*) and general wealth (*vitta*).
The *Akṣarābhidhāna* lexicon defines *ro* as fire, attainment, and a cloud.

Alternatively, one for whom wealth (*dhana*) does not exist is *adhana*, meaning a pauper; for such a person in times of distress, there are streams (*dhārāḥ*) of riches (*rāyaḥ*), which constitute the state of possessing wealth. By means of the worship of the rays, even a pauper becomes endowed with wealth. Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are "at once" (*sapadi*)—meaning now, during the current Kali age—or else "at once" (*sapadi*) refers to that very moment, at the instant of falling, acting as a support (*karālaṃba*) during the descent (*prapāte*) resulting from sinful actions and the like. They serve as a hand-hold for those who approach the solar rays.

"It does not fall downward. Someone else has remarked sarcastically: "If some other rein, the ray, were held fast somewhere at the time of falling downward, it would stretch out"—as Amara states: *praharakṣuḥ-kiraṇa-pragrahā raśmayaḥ* (the words *prahara*, *akṣu*, *kiraṇa*, and *pragraha* are synonyms for *raśmi*).

Furthermore, what are they like? They are the sole lamps for the light of reality (*tattva*). Reality is Brahman; its "light" is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). In that light of reality, they are the supreme lamps or the peerless lamps. Through the worship of the solar rays, the direct realization of Brahman occurs. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *eka* denotes number, but it means 'supreme' when singular, and 'alone' when used in the neuter. Furthermore, what are they like? They are the pathways leading to the city of the Lord of the Third Heaven (*tridivapati*). Thus, the Lord of the Third Heaven is Indra.

Before him stands heaven, the city of the Lord of the Three Worlds; there, the paths for travel are to be sought only by those who worship the rays of the sun, for it is said in the scriptures that they alone are capable of going to heaven, or rather, that the journey to heaven occurs by way of the solar rays. Furthermore, what are they like?

They act as gatekeepers at the door of their own bodies for the yogi striving toward Nirvana—Nirvana being liberation—and who is such a yogi? One who has exerted effort (*udyogin*) therein and is a practitioner of yoga (*yogī*). Thus, he is a "yogi striving toward Nirvana."

His departure is death; immediately thereafter, in the next birth, his own body—his very self—is the gateway to Śiva. As they proceed there, the women seem to ward him off, for the Amarakośa states that *mūrti*, *tanu*, and *tanū* all mean "body."
Furthermore, the rays of the sun prevent rebirth; rather, the meaning is that they lead only to liberation. As it has been said: "There are only two in this world who pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant endowed with yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle."
The meaning is that, just as a doorkeeper holds a special cane (vetra) in his hand to ward off people who have entered the doorway, this [tree] likewise possesses a collection [of branches];
it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. //11//

"May they act accordingly" (*praciprāgiti*): O *caṇḍarocis*, O splendors of the sun, may you fulfill—that is, accomplish in a manner suited to and corresponding with—your thoughts, that is, the desires of the mind. *Caṇḍarociḥ* refers to the sun, whose radiance (*rociḥ*)—meaning light or rays—is fierce (*caṇḍa*) and intense (*tīvra*). Regarding *rucaḥ*, [the lexicon states]: "The words *prabhā*, *dīpti*, and *rociḥ* denote luster; both *rociḥ* and *śociḥ* are neuter," according to Amara.

These eleven names, beginning with *prabhā* and ending with *rociḥ*, spoken by Amarasimha, are synonyms for "luster" (*dīpti*) and also signify "rays. Kaliṅga states that because they illuminate objects, they are synonyms for "that which produces luster. Furthermore, what kind of rays are they? They are "intense rays" (*caṇḍarocīrucaḥ*), being non-final because it is the time of dawn; [this refers to] the morning time.

Not the western [mountain], for Amara states: "The last, the lowest, the final, the end, the western, and the west. Furthermore, what are they like? They are those who, at the eastern mountain—the mountain of sunrise—meaning in the east, at dawn, for a short time (*anaticiram*), that is, for a brief duration, act as, or assume the state of, a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇitvam*); a crest-jewel is a head-ornament, according to Amara. Of what nature is this state of being a crest-jewel? Or rather, it is a beautiful crest-jewel (*cārucūḍāmaṇi*).

The state of that [sun] is "the condition of being a beautiful crest-jewel" (*cārucūḍāmaṇitvam*); this is either a noun or an adverbial modifier meaning "in such a way as to be beautiful. Furthermore, what are they like? They are the quarters of space (*diśām*) which, in their connection with the sun, seem—as if—to discharge abundant, copious *rocanāmbu*, the water of yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), for the sake of chewing [it], for the sake of equal splendor, and for the sake of anointing; and just as the rays of the fierce-rayed one (*caṇḍarocīrucaḥ*) are reddish in color, so too the quarters of space become reddish in color—this is the meaning.

Saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and other such substances are compared to a reddish hue. Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are being honored with eyes—the eyes of *cakravāka* birds that do not possess the name "wheel" (*acakra*)—in a manner that is skillful and full of respect; that is, they are being gazed upon joyfully. Of what nature are those eyes? They are characterized by affectionate words of endearment (*cāṭūkta*). Again, of what nature are they? They are unwavering and steady. The reason for this respect is that at night the *cakravāka* birds are separated from their mates, whereas during the day they will be reunited. //12//

Beginning with one and ending with ten, he describes the rays of the sun under the guise of words denoting numbers, starting with "one": "those [rays] of Bhānu, the Sun— ten times a hundred rays multiplied by the number of sounds (thirty-six)."

That is to say, numbering one thousand; the grammatical construction is that they "may bestow" (dadhatu) welfare and auspiciousness upon you. Which ones? Those which cause the ten hundred rays—that is, the multitude of lights—to contemplate, or rather to attain, as one non-dual essence consisting of light and splendor.

Since all objects in the world become visible at the rising of the sun and so forth, it is appropriate to call the eye "the one light. Furthermore, what are they? They are those proclaimed and celebrated by the four mouths—the faces—of the Lotus-born (Abjaja), that is, Brahmā. Furthermore, what are they? They are those which attain the number five among the elements (bhūta)—earth, water, fire, air, and ether; that is, they become fivefold through the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) within the five elements.

Furthermore, what are those? They are the various kinds [of rays] that proceed in such a manner, excessively and abundantly, during the six seasons beginning with winter, distinguished by differences such as being dull or moderate. Furthermore, what are those? They are the seven [rays] beginning with Marīci, which are praised by the seventy-three sages. 13 is incomplete.

They are neither excessively cold nor excessively hot; even other sick persons become tranquil immediately after drinking them. According to tradition, the sun takes up water in the summer and pours it down during the rains. Regarding the potency of poison in *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) and the like, the color of liquids such as bitter ones, the various divisions of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), and the tastes such as pungent and so forth—this is the exposition.
(14) [Incomplete] He describes the rays by way of their resemblance to a beard (*śmaśru*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "May the one possessing a thousand rays (*daśasatī*) of the sun—whose heat (*gharma*) consists of glowing rays (*tviṣaḥ*)—grant and bestow upon you (*vaḥ*) protection (*śarma*), that is, happiness. Regarding the words: *gharma* refers to heat; *tviṣaḥ* means rays. The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *gharma* may denote the summer season (*ātaye*) or the water of sweat and heat.
The *Prakāśa* lexicon states: "*bhāḥ* (feminine) denotes splendor or a ray."
*Śarma*, *śāta*, and *sukha* mean happiness (Amara).

A collection of ten hundreds is a *daśaśatī*; the suffix *īp* is applied here according to the rule for *dvigu* compounds. Of what nature is this *daśaśatī* of lights? It is like a row of *śmaśru*—that is, a line (*śreṇī*) of the facial hair that grows on a man's face; "the growth of body hair (*tanuruha*) and the beard (*śmaśru*) on a man's face" (Amara).

Furthermore, of what nature were they? They were spreading a state of beauty that was exceedingly sweet and delightful through the light of the quarters of space. The "quarters" (diśaḥ) are themselves like "brides of the quarters" (digvadhvaḥ), meaning women; their "light" (ālokaḥ)—referring to their radiance—is "sweet" (madhuraḥ), meaning pleasing to the heart, and "exceedingly" (samadhikaḥ), meaning surpassing all others. Thus, it is "sweet light" (madhurālokaḥ), and by means of that, they were spreading a "delightful" (ramyām), that is, charming, "state" (avasthām), meaning splendor. They were expanding that [splendor].

The line of young women’s facial hair (*śmaśruśreṇī*) also brings about a state that is more intensely sweet and delightful to behold. In this context, it creates a condition that is both exceedingly sweet and a "sweet light" (*madhurāloka*), meaning pleasant to look upon; thus, it spreads a state that is beautiful because of that. It is fitting that for women who have attained youth, their appearance becomes as pleasant to look upon as a man's beard. According to Amara, *āloka* means "sight" or "vision" (*āloko darśane ghātau*). And according to Rudra, the words *svāda* and *priya* are used for "sweetness," while *madhura* refers to the *śatapuṣpaka* flower.

Alternatively, by making a word-division (*padaviśleṣa*) as *samadhika-madhurā*, [the meaning is]: what kind is the thousandfold radiance of the beams? It is "exceedingly sweet" (*samadhika-madhurā*) because it possesses an extremely pleasing luminosity for the women who are the quarters of the world. The row of beards (*śmaśruśreṇi*) is also exceedingly sweet (*samadhika-madhurā*) for the women because of its state of being excessively dear due to youth. In this interpretation, what else is he like? He bears a beautiful condition or splendor that is common to both worlds—people and the quarters. Furthermore, what else is he like? The thousandfold radiance has ascended; and it is that which has burst forth, with its tawny hue intensified by a trace of maturity.

And because it has become somewhat mature, its tawny hue—the state of being tawny-colored—is intensified; thus, in the compound "udbhinna-prauḍhileśotkalita-kapilimā," the suffix *ana* is applied according to the rule *an-antāt trap-pratyayaḥ*. Even the line of beard, becoming somewhat mature, turns tawny in color. Furthermore, what is it like? It is a singular ornament (*kevalā ekaikālaṅkṛtiḥ*), serving as an equal adornment for both.

Furthermore, of what nature were they? At the "mouth of the day" (dinamukhe)—that is, at dawn—they were slightly emerging, having just begun to appear even upon the rows of beards on the faces of men; here there is a pun (*śleṣa*) with the word "mouth. At that "mouth of the day," which possessed the splendor (*dyuti*) of blossoming lotus-eyes (*ambhojanetra*), where the lotuses themselves were the eyes and those eyes were fully opened (*ujjṛmbha*);
it is fitting that the faces of men also become endowed with the beauty of eyes and mouths at such a time. //15//
Since even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva offer praise, he says:
"Of the moon upon his crest" (maulindoḥ). May that rising—the emergence—of the rays of the sun, the enemy of darkness, be for your protection and preservation.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May that [sun] be for you. Although the word *tviṣ* also denotes a ray of light, as was previously mentioned, what kind of "emergence of rays" (*tviṣāṃ samudgamaḥ*) is it? It is one that is "thin" (*tanu*), meaning extremely subtle, because it belongs to the early morning. That emergence of rays which has been "adequately praised" (*alam... stutaḥ*)—meaning highly extolled—by the Creator (*dhātrā*), namely Brahmā; that is the subject. This connects with the preceding clause. By what kind of Creator? By one who is "seated comfortably within the cave-like interior of a lotus whose petals have just opened" (*pratyagrodghāṭitāmbhoruhakuharaguhāsusthitenaiva*). "Just opened" (*pratyagrodghāṭita*) means recently manifested; and that which is a lotus (*ambhoruha*) is "the lotus whose petals have just opened" (*pratyagrodghāṭitāmbhoruha*).
Its interior cavity is that very same mountain cave and ravine;
by one staying therein, it is as if one were abiding in happiness.

At the rising of its rays, it is the cause for praise because it illuminates the lotus that is its own abode. Furthermore, who is he? He who was praised by Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu. By what kind of Kṛṣṇa? By one who, like darkness (*dhvānta*), overcomes the body of the blackness (*kṛṣṇatva*) [of ignorance]. Like darkness, [he is] as if [dark].

She is Kṛṣṇā, and her own body is black in color. Her defeat—that is, the humiliation—of that [body] by the rising rays [of the sun], as if out of fear because its enemy, darkness, is being destroyed, becomes the cause for praise. Furthermore, for the reason that "this emergence of the mass of rays may not steal (mā amoṣīt)—that is, may not take away—the luster (dyuti), the beauty, of my crest-moon, the moon situated upon my crown," [she was protected] by Mahādeva, whose emblem is the bull.

When the word *muṣasteya* is employed [in the compound] *stuta-muṣasteya*, there is the elision of the suffix *aṭ*. By what kind of one? By the one marked with the bull (*vṛṣabhāṅka*), who is as if possessed by doubt (*śaṅkin*) at the rising of the rays—doubting, "Will this [sun] steal the splendor of the moon on my crest? The cause of the praise is the doubt that the beauty of the moon situated upon his own crest might perish. //16//

He says that the rays of the sun pervade everywhere: "vistrīṇantu. The connection [of the words] is as follows: may the thousand-fold rays (*usra*) of the sun—that is, its beams—quickly (*drutam*), meaning as swiftly as possible, cause (*viśrasayantu*) your undesirable (*anabhimatam*), that is to say, inauspicious things and so forth, to fall away (*vidhvaṃsayantu*). [The root] *śraṃsu* (in the form *dhvaṃsu*) means to fall down. He is one whose rays (*tviṣaḥ*) are thousandfold (*sahasram*), that is, numbering one thousand; of him.
*Dīdhiti*, *bhānu*, *usra*, *aṃśu*, *gabhasti*, *kiraṇa*, and *kara*—these, according to Dhanañjaya, are synonyms for "ray.
What are they? That which is *usra* (the dawn-ray) destroys—that is, dispels—the *tamiśrāṇi* (thick darknesses) at *uṣas* (dawn), that is, at the time of morning, [causing] the lotuses to bloom.

The lotus grove, the world, and the universe shine forth from him; this is the connection [of the verse]. By which rays (*usra*)? Of what nature? Those which, at that very moment (*sapadi*), make the sky (*vyoma*) expansive—that is, they extend it—since at the rising of the rays the entire sky becomes manifest. Again, of what nature? Those which make the ten directions long and wide because they have illuminated them. Again, of what nature? Those which cause the oceans (*achīn*) to have their waters overflowing their shores (*vyasta-velāmbhas*).

"Velā" means the shore of the ocean, and "ambhaḥ" means water; those for whom these two—the shore and the water—are distinct and separated are "velāmbhasī-vyasta-bhinnāḥ. At the rising of the rays, there is a distinction between the surface of the shore and the water at the time of the tide, as Rudra states: "The two banks undergo a transformation at the time of the tide. He describes the rays as being superior even to a lamp, saying: "Empty of scatteredness. May that rising—the emergence—of the rays (arciṣām) of the sharp-rayed (tigmabhānoḥ) sun in the eastern direction (śātakratavyām), which belongs to Śatakratu [Indra], bestow auspiciousness and welfare upon you. Regarding the word *śātakratavī*: it is that which belongs to him (*asya*) who is Śatakratu; in that [direction]. He whose rays (*bhānavaḥ*) are sharp (*tigmāḥ*), or rather, he who is both sharp (*tigmaḥ*) and a ray (*bhānuḥ*)—that is the sun—is *tigmabhānuḥ*. Of him. According to Dhanañjaya: "Pāda, ruci, marici, bhāḥ, tejaḥ, arcis, dyuti, and prabhā [are synonyms for light]."

Of what kind was the sun? He was one whose emergence of rays had attained the name "nine" (*nava*) in relation to both direction and time. "Direction" refers to the east and so forth; "time" refers to the morning. In relation to—that is, with respect to—these two, it had attained the name "new," meaning the number nine. It did not, however, attain the number nine in any other direction or at any other time.

The connection is as follows: "He who is that source of rays, capable and able to make the entire world free from darkness—what is he like? Like a lamp-chamber; just as a lamp-chamber is capable of making itself free from darkness, so is he. What kind of lamp is it?
