"O Ambha, you are devoid of *astavyastatva* (the state of being cast down and destroyed) because you do not perish; by whom could you be cast down? Thus, *asta* means 'cast down' and *vyasta* means 'destroyed'; the state of these two is *astavyastatva*, and you are empty of that. Furthermore, the lamp is indeed possessed of *astavyastatva*:
*asta* means 'thrown down' or 'gone,' as per the *Viśva* lexicon (*astaṃ kṣipte gate prāptam*).

Moreover, what is it like? It is self-luminous (*nijarujaḥ*), shining by itself and not from another, and it is imperishable (*avināśaḥ*), meaning it exists. As for the lamp, however, it is not self-luminous, but rather [shines] through others, such as the supply of oil."

Furthermore, what is its nature? It is "aniśānaśvaraḥ," meaning it does not perish during the day (aniśāyām), that is to say, it is non-destructible and remains present; whereas a lamp, due to its lack of luster during the day, is indeed subject to destruction. //18//

To explain how the rays of the sun descend upon cities such as Pātāla, he says: "May he come. May that mass of light protect you—may that *rociroghaḥ*, a flood (*ogha*) or succession of rays (*rociḥ*), shield you. The word *rociḥ* is also a synonym for a ray. As it is said: "The word *kaliṅga* [is used] for a multitude, a torrent of water, and in the instruction on rapid dancing."
"Ogha" means "succession" according to the *Viśva* lexicon.

Of what nature is this mass of light? It belongs to the "scorcher," the sun (*tapana*). Who is he? He is that mass of light which, having encircled the world-encircler—the mountain range surrounding the earth with its seven continents like a rampart—does not scorch, nor illuminate, the far side, the rear portion of that mountain.

For what purpose? For the sake of its name—that is, for the purpose of explaining the name of that Lokāloka mountain, and for that reason, one side of that mountain is illuminated by the rays of the sun while the other side is unilluminated; therefore, it possesses the literal name "Lokāloka" (Light-and-Darkness). If the sun were to shine upon both sides, the name would be inappropriate; thus, it does not shine upon the far side. This is a figurative expression of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). What is he like?

"Soft and delicate like a lotus fiber (mṛṇālī), that is, soft as a lotus stalk—may the body of the serpents not go to withering, may it not reach a state of decay due to the heat of my rays. Out of compassion alone, out of pity, he did not enter or go to the world of serpents, the netherworld (pātāla); nor did he go to the world of the snakes (ahi-loka), which is the realm of the suns.

Furthermore, what is he like? At the limit of heaven—that is, at the boundary of the sky—above, on high, his height is free from the fear of the bursting of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). A "fragment of the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍakhaṇḍa*) refers to a particular celestial realm; the "fear of its bursting" (*sphuṭanabhaya*) is the apprehension of its shattering, and his height is "abandoned by that," meaning it is devoid of such apprehension. Thus he is described.

Furthermore, what is he like? He is one for whom the limit of space—that is, the boundary of the manifestation of space—is subject to his own will; he is thus one whose limit of space is dependent upon his own desire. //19//

Since the light of the moon and others dissolves upon the rising of the sun’s splendor, he says: "May that which is stainless... May that *dhāman*—the radiance or light of the Lord of Day, the Sun—bestow (*diśatu*) upon you (*vaḥ*) more than your desires (*kāmādhikam*). That is, may it grant even more than what is desired (*īpsitāt*), or even that which is unasked for; or rather, may it grant *kam*, meaning happiness (*sukham*). How is that *kam*? It is "more than desire" (*kāmādhika*), meaning that from which no thought (*dhīḥ*) regarding desires—such as wealth, sons, and so forth—is absent. Thus, it is *kam*.

The meaning is that it is the bliss of the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*). Alternatively, it is that bliss from which there arises no mental anguish (*ādhi*) regarding desires such as wealth, sons, and so forth; for the *Viśva* lexicon states that *dhāma* means "in the body," "in the house," or "in a ray."
"Dīpi" means light; "mahodāma" means wealth-conquering (Dhananjaya);

"sukha-śīrṣa-jale suptam" means sleeping in the water of bliss—thus says the Viśva lexicon. Of what nature is that abode? It is worthy of being beheld at dawn, in the early morning, because of my state of being; it is capable of being seen. When? At that time when that abode is rising, when it emerges; furthermore, when the darkness has vanished and departed, the time is certainly the moment of sunrise. Indeed, it is not the case that it is "ekapadaṃ vā aśyāmaḥ"—it does not become dark for even a single step. On the contrary, it is "aśyāma" indeed: that in which "śyāmā," meaning night, does not exist. "Kṣaṇadā," "rajanī," and "naktaṃ" all mean night.
According to the *Candrapradyota*, Dhanañjaya states that "aśyāmākṣapākara" means "the destroyer of the darkness of faults.

Alternatively, it means that in which there is no *śyāma* (darkness), i.e., *aśyāma*, due to the absence of gloom. What kind of Time (*kāla*) is it? It is "one" (*eka*), meaning preeminent because of its luminosity. Not only is Time itself *aśyāma*, but even the interior of the worlds (*bhuvanānta*) is *aśyāma*; it does not become dark, but remains *aśyāma*. Here, the particle *na* is for the purpose of negation. Alternatively, *aśyāmaḥ* does not mean "not black," but rather "it is not like *a-śyāma*"—that is, it is not black-colored like *a* (Kṛṣṇa). In this interpretation, the particle *na* serves as a prohibition.
That which is called "A" is the single-syllable designation for Viṣṇu.

Furthermore, what is that? It is that state (dhāman) upon reaching whose emergence the mountain Himālaya—that immovable foot—does not immediately go to dissolution or scatter at that very moment; rather, it certainly does go [to dissolution]. Even the moon (candramas) does not go to dissolution or wither; rather, it certainly does go [to dissolution]. There is no cause for doubt even in this regard.

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of including the head [in the list]. Furthermore, in which abode (*dhāman*) is it that at the rising of the sun, the *siddhāñjali*s—the joined palms (*karasaṃpuṭa*) of the *siddhas*, a specific class of divine beings—do not form a *vandha* (a binding)? They certainly do; at the rising of the solar abode, the *siddhas* join their palms in salutation (*praṇāmārtha*). Likewise, for the bed of night-lotuses (*kumudavana*), the "sealing" (*mudraṇa*) does not fail to occur;
rather, it certainly does. Thus, the particle *na* is used solely for the purpose of including the head. //20//
He describes the splendor of the sun by means of its unique quality as the eye:
"That radiance which... The blazing majesty (*mahaḥ*) of the sun—may that be for you a destroyer of evil, a dispeller of misfortune.
Alternatively, "agham" means misfortune (*vyasanam*), that is to say, despicable action; may they destroy that. Or, "agham" means suffering (*duḥkham*); may they cause that to perish.
For the *Viśvaprakāśa* states: "Agha is said to be misfortune; agha refers to both evil and suffering.
And the *Viśva* states: "Mahaḥ occurs in the sense of great and splendor (*tejaḥ*)."
Of what nature is that light? It is the one, unique eye of the three worlds—that is, of the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavenly realms—because it illuminates them;
indeed, that light is like no ordinary eye.

He describes a distinct and extraordinary difference between us ordinary people and his eyes: what is that splendor which is the eye of the three worlds and which does not steal away the beauty and luster of the lotuses?

She makes [the lotuses] distant; however, she makes them exceedingly beautiful—exceedingly (*atyantam*) and excessively (*adhikam*) beautiful—so that they might become rivals for her. But our eyes steal the splendor of the lotuses; therefore, she does not make them exceedingly beautiful.
Furthermore, according to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *atyartha* means "excessively" or "in a high degree.

Now, which of these two is that great light—the eye of the three worlds—which does not merely fail to nourish or sustain the splendor (*tārakā-bhām*) of the stars (*nakṣatra-śobhām*), but rather excessively, quickly, and perpetually eclipses it? For the eye of people such as ourselves possesses the splendor of the pupil (*kanīnikā-śobhā*), and for that very reason, it outshines them. Here, the word *tārakā* is used ironically (*chala-ukti*) to refer to the pupil. [The word *tārakā* refers to the pupil.]
The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *tāraka* means both a star and the pupil of the eye.
The *Amarakośa* also says: "*Tāraka* is the eye; it is the pupil (*kanīnikā*).

Furthermore, that light which is the eye of the three worlds is not capable—that is, not able—to perform a closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*), but rather it is solely capable of performing a day. However, the eye of those such as ourselves is not capable of performing a day, but is indeed capable of performing a closing of the eyes.
"Kevala" means "supreme" according to the Viśva lexicon; alternatively, "eternal" or "indestructible" is an epithet of "maha," and "supreme" or "most excellent" is also an epithet of "maha. //21//
Because the splendor of the sun travels everywhere, he says:

"May the splendor of the sun, which traverses the earth swiftly, burn away—that is, destroy—the ill omen, the cause of misfortune, for you. Of what nature is that splendor? It is as if it were eager to touch the surface of the waters of the night with its exceedingly cool rays; thus, may it traverse the earth most rapidly.

They have reached the surface of the world, which is extremely cool—more so than the dewy water (*kṣapāmbhas*)—due to the fact that the verbal roots denoting "to go" (*gati*) also carry the sense of "to reach" (*prāpti*). Because there is an absence of thirst (*atarṣaḥ*) upon touching its surface, which is cooled by the dewy water, they are as if free from the desire for touch caused by that contact with the surface cooled by the dewy water. (In the word *kṣapīyas*, the suffix *iyasun* is added in the sense of excellence;

*tarṣaḥ* is the state of being thirsty, meaning desire; according to Amara, *kṣā*, *spṛhā*, *ambhaḥ*, and *tṛṭ* are synonyms). Furthermore, what kind [of beings] are they? They are those who have reached the elephants of the quarters (*āśā-diggaja*).

The trunk is the hand; that itself is the lake of lotuses (*puṣkariṇī*). As if to awaken—that is, to bring to consciousness—the "lotuses," meaning the tips [of the trunk], the solar radiance has quickly reached the quarters of the sky. It is as if the sun's light has arrived to illuminate other lotuses (*puṣkara*) as well. This is a pun (*śleṣa*) based on the word *puṣkara*.

According to Rudra: "In water, at the tip of an elephant’s trunk, in the sky, a sword, a plough, a lotus, a sacred ford, and a drum—these are the meanings of *puṣkara*; and the face of the Sun is also called *puṣkara*."

Furthermore, of what nature was she? At dawn, as if out of loathing or contempt—that is to say, with utter disregard—she leaped over even the station of Viṣṇu, that is, the station of the sky, by means of her extreme speed. Shining intensely in the far distance, "uddāmadyotamānā" means both unrestrained and brilliantly radiant. The word "pada" is used here by way of an allusion (kaṭākṣita), for just as anyone else might walk away after stepping over a footprint or a mark of Kama and the like due to disgust because it is stuck there;
for the word *pada* signifies sound, a foot, effort, and instruction. (Amara-kośa 3.3.19).
"According to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *pāda* refers to the feet, marks, place, protection, and the sun;
or rather, by *ghṛṇā*—meaning compassion (*kṛpā*)—she who shines intensely within [the heart] brings benefit to all at the rising of the sun.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, *ghṛṇā* means both loathing (*jugupsā*) and compassion (*kṛpā*). //22//
He describes the splendor of the sun by way of its being a lamp that dispels dejection:
"nokalpāpāyavāyoḥ" and so forth.

May the radiance (*dīpti*)—the light (*vavarti*)—of the hot-rayed (*uṣmatviṣaḥ*) sun bring you happiness; may it make you blissful. The compound *dīptivavartiḥ* is a *vyastarūpakālaṅkāra* (a metaphor with separated members): *varttiḥ* refers to the wick (*dīpadaśā*), which is the part of the lamp that is smeared with oil. Of what kind [is the sun]? Of the "hot-rayed," who is the lamp (*dīpaḥ*) for all the continents (*nikhiladvīpa*), meaning the illuminator (*pradīpaḥ*) of all the continents such as Jambūdvīpa, Hastidvīpa, and so on—he is the "lamp of all continents."

Of what nature is this? It is a wick that is indeed a flame (*dīpti*), having a different form—that is to say, of a different appearance—distinct from the characteristics of an ordinary lamp. He states its distinction: "that flame which is the wick" belongs to the one for whom the mountain ranges (*kṣmādhara*) have been shattered and pulverized by the fierce force (*adaya-raya*) of his speed (*adaya*); *adaya* means fierce, and *raya* means velocity; thus, *adaya-raya*. By that [force], the mountain ranges are shattered and reduced to dust. An ordinary lamp, however, is extinguished even by a slight breeze; such is the distinction.
Because of the necessary connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word *yā* (which) must be understood.

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It does not become one whose brilliant splendor (*ujjvala-śrī*) is intensely emitted during the day; rather, it is precisely one whose brilliant splendor remains intensely emitted—this is the rhetorical emphasis (*śiraścāraṇa*). That which is both brilliant (*ujjvalā*) and splendor (*śrīḥ*), or beauty, is "brilliant splendor" (*ujjvala-śrī*); that which is both emitted (*udgīrṇṇā*, i.e., manifested) and brilliant splendor is "emitted brilliant splendor" (*udgīrṇṇojjvala-śrī*); and that which is both intense (*gāḍhā*, i.e., excessive) and emitted brilliant splendor is "intensely emitted brilliant splendor" (*gāḍhodgīrṇṇojjvala-śrī*). For a lamp that is clearly visible becomes utterly devoid of luster during the day; this is the distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*). Furthermore, of what nature is it?

Darkness is indeed soot (*kajjala*); it is not the case that [the lamp] is devoid of—that is, abandoned by—it; rather, on the contrary, even a well-known lamp, merely by its movement over the wick, is possessed of soot.

The distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*) is as follows: Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is "one whose birth was obtained from the *pataṅga*," that is, from the sun (*sūrya*). Moreover, she has not undergone destruction (*moṣa*), meaning ruin, from the sun. For the well-known radiance of a lamp, however, its origin was not obtained from the *pataṅga*—the bird—for a bird meets with destruction; indeed, some bird extinguishes a lamp with its two wings. Thus, by means of a pun on the word *pataṅga*, the distinction is established. According to the *Utpalinī*: "The word *pataṅga* refers to the moth, the bird, and the sun. (23)

He describes the color of the rays through their similarity to *ruc* (splendor/desire): "Filling all directions without remainder. The *ruci*—meaning the rays or, alternatively, the splendor—of *bradhna*, the sun; or rather, [the *ruci*] of you (*vaḥ*), meaning its brilliance (*abhīpti*); may that be for the attainment (*āptaye*) of that object, that thing. According to the *Unādi-sūtra*: "Sūra, Sūrya, Aryaman, Bradhna, Dvādaśātman, and Vikartana [are names of the Sun].
The *Viśva-prakāśa* lexicon states: "*Ruci* means a ray (*mayūkha*), splendor (*śobhā*), attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), and desire (*abhilāṣa*)."

Who is she? She who is the radiance of the sun (bradhna), perfected like radiance itself, blazing and manifested here in accordance with her desire; for the word *tacchupta* is to be understood as *tat-chapta* (blazing from that). Furthermore, what is her nature? She whose form is to be praised for its preeminent and weighty qualities, which completely fulfill all desires.

She whose own form (svarūpa) is worthy of praise and eulogy because of her preeminent and exalted virtues—virtues which are the supreme fulfillment of all desires and hopes (niḥśeṣāśā) without exception; and who, at the beginning of the day, at dawn, neither rises nor expands excessively, but rather [shines] sufficiently and according to her will, like the radiance of the sun (bradhna).
Furthermore, what kind of splendor of the sun (bradhna-ruci) is it? It is that which is "elevated even at the time of the day's departure" (dinagama-samayopaplava);
that is, even at the end of the day, it is not merely elevated, but is indeed elevated—referring to the "departure" (gama), meaning the progression, of the day (ahnaḥ).
*Samayaḥ* means time; *upaplavaḥ* means destruction. In that [time], namely during childhood and old age, his power is diminished (*valitā*).
[The word] *tuyartheṣṭe* means "sufficiently" or "enough," according to the *Viśva* lexicon.

Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is the radiance of the sun (bradhna), which does not abide—meaning it does not stay—even for a moment, that is, for any brief duration, together with darkness; she has utterly transcended it, as it were, never having coexisted with darkness at any time.
But the meaning is that it is precisely the destruction of darkness [that occurs]. //24//

In imitation of Kārttikeya, he describes the rays [of the sun] with the verse beginning "bibhrāṇaḥ. May the heat, the light, or the ray of the Lord of Day (aharpateḥ), that is, the Sun, bestow upon you (vaḥ) boundless (apārām), immeasurable prosperity (lakṣmīm) or wealth; or alternatively, may it produce beauty (lakṣmīm)—that is to say, the splendor of the body. For it is said in the *Utpalinī*: "A ray (kiraṇaḥ), a beam (dīdhitih), radiance (dīptiḥ), the glow of dawn (prabhātadyotaḥ), and heat (ātapaḥ)."
According to Amara, *prakāśa*, *udyota*, and *ātapa* mean light.

In the case of *Haripriyā* (the beloved of Hari), she is like *lakṣmī* or *śrī*, the goddess of fortune and beauty; thus she is called *utpalinī*. What is this heat (*ātapa*) like? It is like another, a second *guha*, that is, Kārttikeya. How is the heat characterized? He characterizes both by means of an adjective. In the case of the heat, what is it doing? While bringing about an exceeding, surpassing passion of the eyes for those who look upon it in the darkness of night, it brings joy to the eyes of people at the rising of the sun. "Vikṣaṇam" marks the end of the first canto. // 1 //
